los.description: Implement linear models with interactions and splines and report average marginal effects with intervals, given household consumption with tariff band, household size and temperature
Apply logistic and count models, choosing between Poisson and negative binomial from a dispersion check, given late-payment flags and weekly leak reports with pipe length as exposure
Diagnose misfit with residuals, influence measures and simulation from the fitted model, then correct the model, given a model with five seeded problems such as overdispersion and separation
Analyse grouped data with clustered standard errors and a random-intercept model and explain how the intervals change, given readings nested in 30 districts of very different sizes
Apply ridge and lasso with cross-validated tuning and measure the stability of the selected predictors, given 120 correlated candidate predictors

Build and defend a regression model for a planner's question, justifying terms, family, uncertainty and whether the use is descriptive, predictive or causal, given a supplied dataset and a written brief

questions.prompt: A vendor's late-payment model, trained on 2025 bills, ranks 2026 bills well: 80% of the late payers are in its top fifth. The vendor says sending reminders to that fifth will cut late payment. What does the evidence support?
options: That reminders to the top fifth will cut late payment
That the model predicts which 2026 bills will be paid late
That the model's variables explain why bills are paid late
Nothing, since the model was not tested in a trial
questions.explanation: The model was checked on bills it did not see, which supports prediction. What a reminder changes is a causal question that needs reminders to be sent, ideally at random.
misconceptions: Reads a good ranking as proof of an effect: no reminders were sent, so nothing measured what they change
Treats a prediction as a description of why: a ranking can work through variables that cause nothing
Assumes evidence needs a randomised trial to support any use; checked predictions support prediction

questions.prompt: You simulate bills from a model with a temperature spline, fit the same model and recover every coefficient within its interval; coverage over 200 repeats is 95%. What have you shown?
options: That Sahil's real bills follow a temperature spline
That the temperature effect is causal
That the real model's intervals will cover 95%
That the code and the estimator work when the model is right
questions.explanation: You planted the model, so recovering it checks the fitting machinery only. Whether real data follow it is a separate check against the data.
misconceptions: Confuses recovering a planted model with the real data following it
Reads coverage as a property of the effect, not of the interval method
Assumes the real data share the fake data's noise; real residuals may fan out or cluster

questions.prompt: A planner fits log consumption with a temperature spline, takes exp of each household's prediction for August and sums them to size the district's supply. The total comes out below the meters' August total. What is the most likely reason?
options: exp of a log-scale prediction is a median, which sits below the mean
The spline has too few degrees of freedom to fit August
The interval for the mean was too narrow
Log models cannot be used for volumes
questions.explanation: The mean of the log is below the log of the mean, so exp(prediction) underestimates the mean. Add σ²/2 before exp, or use smearing.
misconceptions: Blames flexibility for a bias that any log model has; the spline's residuals showed no pattern
Confuses the band, which is about uncertainty, with the level of the prediction
Assumes a log model cannot predict totals at all; it can, after the right back-transform

questions.prompt: In a model of log consumption with a band-by-size interaction, the size coefficient is 0.096 and the villa-by-size term is 0.019. Ghaliya asks how many more cubic metres a month go with one more person in villa households. What do you report?
options: 0.019 m³, the villa-by-size term
12.1%, from the summed slope
The average over villa bills of the m³ difference from one more person, with an interval
The standard band's 2.3 m³, since size works the same way
questions.explanation: The question is in m³ for villa households, so the answer is computed on that scale and averaged over those bills: about 5.0 m³ (4.8 to 5.2).
misconceptions: Reads the interaction term alone as the villa slope; it is a difference between slopes
Stops at the log scale: a percentage is not the cubic metres she asked for
Ignores the interaction: the reference band's slope does not apply to villas

questions.prompt: A model of log monthly consumption has a size slope of 0.096 for standard households. Ghaliya asks how many more cubic metres a month go with one more person in standard households. What do you give her?
options: About 10% more per person
The average over standard bills of the m³ difference from one more person: about 2.3 (2.3 to 2.4)
exp(0.096) times the median bill
questions.explanation: The question names a scale (m³) and a population (standard households): compute on that scale, average over those bills, and add an interval.
misconceptions: Gives the log-scale coefficient, which is not in cubic metres
Gives a percentage when the question asked for a volume
Uses exp of the prediction, the median, so the volume comes out about 5% too small

questions.prompt: A planner wants the probability that a new connection request is approved within 10 days, from the request's district, type and completeness. About 4% of incomplete requests are approved in time. Which model do you start from?
options: A logistic model of the approved-in-time flag
A linear model of the approved-in-time flag
A linear model of the number of days to approval
A Poisson model of the approved-in-time flag
questions.explanation: The outcome is a flag, so the family is binomial; a rate near 4% is exactly where a straight line breaks.
misconceptions: Ignores that the outcome is a flag: a line can predict below 0 for incomplete requests near 4%
Changes the question: days to approval is another outcome, and the planner asked for a probability
Uses a count model for a yes-or-no outcome

questions.prompt: The autopay odds ratio is 0.10. Without autopay, a household's predicted probability of a late bill is 5%. About how much lower is it for the same profile with autopay?
options: 90 percentage points
25 percentage points
10 percentage points
About 4.5 percentage points
questions.explanation: Odds 0.05/0.95 = 0.053; a tenth is 0.0053, a probability of about 0.5%. From 5% to 0.5% is 4.5 points.
misconceptions: Reads the odds ratio as a multiplier on the probability, then subtracts 90% of 100 points
Applies the average over all bills to a household near the bound
Subtracts the odds ratio from the probability as if both were on one scale

questions.prompt: A colleague fits leak counts on material and age with a Poisson model and no offset. Segments of asbestos cement happen to be shorter on average. What happens to the asbestos-cement coefficient?
options: Nothing: a Poisson model accounts for length
It compares counts, not rates, so short asbestos-cement mains look less leaky than they are
Its standard error grows, but the estimate is fine
Only predictions change; coefficients are unaffected
questions.explanation: Without the exposure, a coefficient describes counts per segment; shorter segments have fewer chances to leak, which hides a higher rate.
misconceptions: Assumes the model adjusts for length by itself; without an offset or a length term it cannot
Confuses exposure with dispersion: length changes the mean, not the variance-to-mean ratio
Thinks an offset only matters for prediction, not for the coefficients

questions.prompt: A Poisson model of leak counts has a Pearson dispersion of 2.3. Its rate ratio for asbestos cement is 1.62 with a 95% interval of 1.38 to 1.91. What should Basil expect from a negative binomial refit?
options: A much smaller rate ratio, since the Poisson estimate is inflated
The same interval, with a better AIC
A similar rate ratio with an interval about one and a half times as wide
No answer: counts with overdispersion need a zero-inflated model
questions.explanation: Both models describe the same mean; the negative binomial admits the extra variance, which widens the intervals by about the square root of the dispersion.
misconceptions: Thinks overdispersion biases the estimate itself; it mainly understates its uncertainty
Thinks the extra parameter only changes the fit statistics
Confuses overdispersion with excess zeros needing a different model family entirely

questions.prompt: A Poisson leak model with offset log(km-years) gives asbestos cement a rate ratio of 1.62; its dispersion is 2.3. What can Basil's note say?
options: Asbestos-cement mains have 1.62 more leaks a year than PVC mains
Asbestos cement leaks at about 1.6 times the rate of PVC at equal age and pressure, with an interval wider than the Poisson one
Replacing asbestos cement with PVC will cut leaks by 38%
Nothing, because the model is overdispersed
questions.explanation: A rate ratio compares rates per kilometre-year; with dispersion 2.3 the honest interval is about one and a half times as wide, as the negative binomial showed.
misconceptions: Reads a rate ratio as a difference in counts
Thinks the offset makes the comparison causal
Thinks overdispersion makes the estimate unusable rather than its interval too narrow

questions.prompt: For a logistic model of meter faults, binned residuals against meter age are positive for the youngest and oldest meters and negative in between; 6 of 20 bins sit outside the band. What do you do?
options: Nothing: some bins always fall outside
Switch to a Poisson model of faults
Use robust standard errors
Give age a curved term, such as a spline, and plot the binned residuals again
questions.explanation: A U-shaped pattern against one predictor means its effect is not straight on the log odds scale; a flexible term for it is the repair, checked by the same plot.
misconceptions: Thinks a 2-SE band allows many bins outside by chance; about one in 20 is expected
Reaches for a different family when the problem is the form of one predictor
Treats a pattern in the mean as a problem of the standard errors

questions.prompt: In a model of 30 district rates, one district has leverage 0.7 and Cook's distance 1.5. Its data are correct: a new district with unusually high pressure. What goes in the report?
options: Keep it, and report the estimates with and without it, saying the pressure result leans on one district
Delete it as an outlier, since its Cook's distance is above 1
Keep it and say nothing, since the data are correct
Take the log of the leak rate so that it is no longer influential
questions.explanation: A real unit stays in. Because the conclusions depend on it, the reader must see both fits and the reason.
misconceptions: Treats high influence as proof of an error; this district's data were checked and are correct
Hides the influence instead of reporting it; a robust fit still leaves the reader unaware
Thinks a log transform removes influence that comes from the predictors' position

questions.prompt: A Poisson model of complaints per district-month will be used to staff the call centre for the busiest months. You can simulate 1,000 replicate years from it. Which statistic makes the most useful check?
options: The total number of complaints in the year
The mean temperature of the months
The largest monthly count in any district
The coefficient of temperature
questions.explanation: Staffing depends on the peaks, and a Poisson model with too little variance under-produces them; the total says nothing.
misconceptions: Uses a statistic the model reproduces by construction, so the check cannot fail
Checks the predictors' distribution, which the model does not generate
Uses the fitted coefficients themselves, which replicate exactly by definition

questions.prompt: A logistic model of whether a customer cancels includes "closing letter printed". Its coefficient is 31 with a standard error of 9,000, and the model's AIC is far better than without it. What is the likely explanation?
options: The letter is by far the strongest driver of cancelling
The letter is printed only for customers who cancel, so it separates the outcome and must be removed
The sample is too small; collect more months
Use HC3 standard errors and keep the term
questions.explanation: A huge coefficient with a huge standard error points to separation; a flag created by the outcome is leakage as well, so no estimation method rescues it.
misconceptions: Reads a runaway coefficient as a very strong real effect
Treats a structural problem as a sampling one that more data would solve
Uses robust errors for a problem of the estimate itself

questions.prompt: A colleague's logistic model of meter faults is ready for review. Which entry would an assessor accept?
options: The residuals looked a bit off, so I added a log term
No problems: the model converged without warnings
Missing curve: 6 of 20 binned residuals against meter age outside the 2-SE band; with a spline in age, 1 of 20
AIC fell by 40, so the model is right
questions.explanation: A log line names the problem, the evidence with its number, and the fix with the evidence that it worked.
misconceptions: Names a feeling, not evidence; nobody can check it
Treats convergence as a check of the model
Uses a fit statistic alone, which says nothing about where the model fails

questions.prompt: A model of 50,000 students' scores in 80 schools has two predictors: hours of homework (per student) and a new curriculum (per school). You switch to errors clustered by school. What happens?
options: Both coefficients change, and both intervals widen
The curriculum's interval widens far more than homework's, and neither estimate changes
Homework's interval widens most, because it has more variation
Nothing much: with 50,000 students clustering does not matter
questions.explanation: The curriculum varies only between 80 schools, so its evidence is 80 schools; homework is compared within every school.
misconceptions: Thinks clustering changes estimates rather than standard errors
Has the direction backwards: the school-level term has fewer independent units
Thinks a large sample makes clustering irrelevant

questions.prompt: In a random-intercept model, district A has 50 bills and a raw mean 0.12 above average; district B has 5,000 bills and the same raw mean. What do their estimated levels look like?
options: Both shrink by the same share, as their raw means are equal
B shrinks more, because it has more bills to average
Neither moves: each district keeps its own mean
A moves noticeably towards the average; B stays almost at 0.12
questions.explanation: The shrinkage factor τ²/(τ² + σ²/n) is close to 1 for large n; a mean from 50 bills is less reliable, so it borrows more from the other districts.
misconceptions: Thinks shrinkage depends on the size of the deviation, not on how much data supports it
Has the direction of shrinkage backwards
Confuses partial pooling with no pooling

questions.prompt: A lasso with a cross-validated penalty selected 25 of 90 predictors. Over 100 bootstrap samples, 6 are selected every time and 40 are selected between 20% and 80% of the time. What can you say?
options: The 25 selected predictors are the drivers of demand
The 6 are a stable core; the others' selection depends on the sample and should not be reported as findings
The model is useless and should be dropped
Lower the penalty until all 40 are always selected
questions.explanation: Selection is itself uncertain; only what survives resampling is a stable choice, and even that is a predictive, not a causal, statement.
misconceptions: Treats one fit's selection as a stable finding
Thinks unstable selection makes the predictions useless
Thinks a smaller penalty fixes instability, when it only selects more

questions.prompt: Households with a smart meter display used less water than comparable households without one. They asked for the displays themselves. Which sentence fits the report?
options: Installing displays will cut demand across Sahil
The display coefficient is −0.07 on the log scale
Households with a display used about 7% less than comparable ones (with its interval); they chose it, so this is not the effect of installing one
Displays save water
questions.explanation: The sentence is descriptive, in the reader's terms, with its uncertainty and its limit stated.
misconceptions: Turns an observational comparison into a causal promise
Reports a log-scale coefficient the reader cannot use
Drops the uncertainty and the comparison it rests on

questions.prompt: A city report fits monthly consumption on tariff band, household size and temperature for all billed households and writes: "The social tariff makes families use 9% less water." Which sentence does the analysis support?
options: Households on the social tariff used about 9% less water than comparable households on other tariffs in the data
Moving a family to the social tariff would cut its use by about 9%
The social tariff caused a 9% saving once size and temperature were controlled
Nothing, because regression on observational data supports no statement
questions.explanation: The data compare different households, so they support a description of the difference between groups, not a claim about what the tariff does.
misconceptions: Reads a comparison between groups of households as the effect of changing one household's tariff
Believes that adjusting for some variables turns a comparison into a causal estimate
Treats descriptive use as worthless: a stated comparison in a stated population is a valid result

questions.prompt: Ghaliya asks: "How much more water does a household with one more person use, in our villa districts?" Which is the estimand?
options: The coefficient of household size in a model of log consumption
The R squared of a model that includes household size
The average difference in monthly cubic metres between villa households and the same households with one more person
The p-value of household size in a model fitted to all bands
questions.explanation: An estimand names the population, the outcome with its unit and the comparison; a coefficient, a fit statistic or a p-value is a property of a model, not the quantity asked about.
misconceptions: Confuses a model's coefficient, on its own scale, with the quantity the question asks for
Takes a measure of fit for an answer to a question about size
Takes a test statistic for the quantity of interest and ignores the population named

questions.prompt: You simulate 200 data sets from a known model, fit each, and find that 81% of the 95% intervals for one coefficient contain its planted value. What does that tell you?
options: The planted value is probably wrong
The intervals are too narrow for this design, so the standard errors or the model are wrong for it
The estimates are biased, so the model should be refitted on real data
Nothing: 81% is within the normal noise of 200 repeats
questions.explanation: With 200 repeats, coverage of a correct 95% interval falls between about 92% and 98%; 81% means the intervals understate the uncertainty.
misconceptions: Forgets that in fake data the planted value is known exactly
Confuses under-coverage with bias: intervals can miss because they are too narrow around unbiased estimates
Overestimates the simulation noise of a coverage count over 200 repeats

questions.prompt: A model that recovers every planted coefficient from fake data has been shown to describe the real bills well.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Recovering a planted model checks the code and the estimator; whether the real data follow the model is checked against the data.
misconceptions: Confuses a test of the method with a test of the model against the world

questions.prompt: A model of log monthly consumption has a residual standard deviation of 0.30. For one household type it predicts 3.00 on the log scale. What is the best estimate of that type's mean consumption?
options: exp(3.00), about 20.1 cubic metres
exp(3.30), about 27.1 cubic metres
3.00 cubic metres
exp(3.045), about 21.0 cubic metres
questions.explanation: With normal errors on the log scale the mean is exp(prediction + sigma squared / 2) = exp(3.00 + 0.045).
misconceptions: Takes the median, exp(prediction), for the mean
Adds sigma instead of sigma squared over two
Forgets to back-transform from the log scale

questions.prompt: A spline fit on 40,000 bills gives a 95% band of 37.3 to 38.4 cubic metres at 40 °C for four-person standard households. A customer of that type disputes a bill of 46 cubic metres. What does the band say about the bill?
options: Nothing direct: the band is for the mean of such households, and single bills spread far wider
The bill is almost certainly a meter error, since it lies outside the band
The bill should be cut to 38.4 cubic metres
The model is wrong, since a real bill falls outside its band
questions.explanation: An interval for the mean narrows as data grow; an interval for one household includes the household-to-household spread and is many times wider.
misconceptions: Reads an interval for the mean as the range of single bills
Uses the mean band as a ceiling for an individual bill
Expects individual observations to fall inside an interval for the mean

questions.prompt: In log_m3 ~ tariff_band * household_size, the household_size coefficient is 0.096 and tariff_band[T.social]:household_size is -0.022. What is the social band's slope for household size on the log scale?
questions.explanation: The reference band's slope plus the social interaction term: 0.096 - 0.022 = 0.074, about 7.7% per person.
misconceptions: Reads the interaction term as the band's slope; it is a difference between slopes
Ignores the interaction and applies the reference band's slope
Adds the size of the interaction instead of its signed value

questions.prompt: On the log scale, one more person goes with 7.6% more consumption on the social band and 12.1% more on the villa band. In cubic metres a month, the villa effect turns out more than three times the social one. Why?
options: The percentages were computed wrongly
The interval for villas is wider
Villas have fewer households in the data
The same percentage applies to a higher base: villas use far more water to begin with
questions.explanation: An effect in cubic metres is the percentage times each household's level, so a larger base turns similar percentages into much larger volumes.
misconceptions: Assumes the two scales must agree in ratio
Confuses the width of an interval with the size of an effect
Confuses the number of rows with the size of an effect

questions.prompt: For each district and month, a utility records the number of meter faults and the number of meters installed. Which model fits the question "how does the fault rate differ by meter age?"
options: A linear model of the number of faults
A logistic model of whether the district had any fault
A Poisson or negative binomial model of faults with log meters as an offset
A linear model of faults divided by meters, without weights
questions.explanation: The outcome is a count with an exposure (meters), so a count model with log exposure as an offset describes the rate per meter.
misconceptions: Treats a count as a continuous outcome, which allows negative predictions and ignores exposure
Throws away the counts by reducing them to a flag
Divides by exposure but treats a rate from 10 meters as exactly as reliable as one from 10,000

questions.prompt: A linear probability model can predict a negative probability for some households even when it fits the average difference well.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: A line subtracts the same amount from every row, so rows that start near zero are pushed below it; the average difference can still be right.
misconceptions: Believes that a model which gets the average right must get every prediction into range

questions.prompt: In a logistic model of late payment, the odds ratio for each past late payment is 1.6. A household has a 20% probability of a late bill. About what is the probability for the same household with one more past late payment?
questions.explanation: Odds 0.2/0.8 = 0.25; times 1.6 is 0.40; a probability of 0.40/1.40, about 29%.
misconceptions: Multiplies the probability by the odds ratio
Adds the odds ratio's excess as percentage points
Adds 16 points as if the odds ratio were a difference on the probability scale

questions.prompt: Bills on autopay were late 40 points less often than comparable bills without it, in a logistic model of observational data. Which sentence may go in the collections report?
options: Comparable households on autopay paid late about 40 points less often than those without it
Enrolling households in autopay will cut their late payment by 40 points
Autopay reduces late payment by 90%, as its odds ratio is 0.1
Autopay causes on-time payment for most households
questions.explanation: Households chose autopay, so the data support a comparison of households, not a statement of what enrolling them would do.
misconceptions: Reads a comparison of self-selected groups as the effect of an action
Reads an odds ratio as a cut in probability and adds a causal claim
Turns an association into a causal claim about most households

questions.prompt: In a Poisson model of leaks with offset log(kilometre-years), the coefficient of pressure is 0.28. What does exp(0.28) = 1.32 mean?
options: Each extra bar goes with 1.32 more leaks a year on every main
Each extra bar goes with 32% more leaks per kilometre-year, other terms equal
Each extra bar adds 0.28 leaks per kilometre
A main at high pressure is 1.32 kilometres longer on average
questions.explanation: With a log link and an exposure offset, exp(coefficient) is a rate ratio per kilometre-year.
misconceptions: Reads a rate ratio as a difference in counts
Reads the log-scale coefficient as a difference in rate
Confuses the offset with an outcome

questions.prompt: A Poisson model of complaints per district-month has a Pearson dispersion of 4.0. A colleague reports a rate ratio for pressure management of 1.40 with a 95% interval of 1.20 to 1.63. What do you tell them?
options: The interval is about right, since dispersion affects only the fit
The estimate is biased upward by a factor of 4
Use a linear model instead, because counts with dispersion are not Poisson
The interval is too narrow; refit with a negative binomial or scale the errors, which roughly doubles its width on the log scale
questions.explanation: With dispersion 4, standard errors are too small by about the square root of 4, so the log-scale interval should be about twice as wide.
misconceptions: Believes overdispersion leaves the uncertainty unchanged
Thinks overdispersion biases the rate ratio by the dispersion factor
Abandons the count family instead of widening the variance

questions.prompt: You plot the raw residuals of a logistic model of late payment against the bill and see two curved bands. What does this tell you about the model?
options: The model needs a quadratic term in the bill
Nothing yet: raw residuals of a yes-or-no outcome always form two bands, so bin and average them first
The model is overdispersed
The bill should be removed from the model
questions.explanation: Each residual is either 1 - p or -p, so two bands appear for any model; only averages of residuals within bins carry information about the fit.
misconceptions: Reads the shape forced by a binary outcome as a missing curve
Borrows a count-model diagnosis for a binary outcome
Treats a plotting artefact as evidence against a predictor

questions.prompt: Binned residuals of a logistic model by fitted probability show 1 of 20 bins outside the band. Against tenure in months, 6 of 20 bins sit outside, all negative for the shortest tenures. What do you conclude?
options: The model fits, since the plot by fitted probability is the standard check
The model is fine, since 6 of 20 is within what chance gives
Tenure's effect is not straight on the log odds scale; try a curved term for it and check again
Remove tenure because its residuals are biased
questions.explanation: Binning by fitted probability mixes all predictors and can average away a misfit in one; 6 of 20 outside against tenure, with a pattern, points to the form of tenure.
misconceptions: Trusts the plot that mixes predictors over the one that isolates the problem
Expects many bins outside by chance, when about one in 20 is typical
Drops a predictor instead of fixing its form

questions.prompt: In a regression on 30 districts, district A has leverage 0.70 and a small residual; district B has leverage 0.08 and a residual five times larger than any other. Which statement is right?
options: A is unusual in its predictors, B in its outcome; either can move the fit, which Cook's distance measures
Only B can be influential, because influence comes from residuals
Only A can be influential, because influence comes from leverage
Both should be deleted before refitting
questions.explanation: Leverage measures how far a unit's predictors are from the rest; influence, as in Cook's distance, combines leverage with the size of the residual.
misconceptions: Ignores the role of leverage in influence
Ignores the role of the residual in influence
Treats flags as rules for deletion

questions.prompt: Two districts with very high Cook's distance turn out to have their main lengths keyed in tens of kilometres. A third influential district is a real new development. What is the right repair?
options: Delete all three and report the fit on 27 districts
Keep all three as they are, since deleting data is never allowed
Correct the two lengths from the source table, keep the new district, and report the fit with and without it
Replace the outcome with its logarithm so that none is influential
questions.explanation: Errors are corrected from the source; real units stay, and when a conclusion leans on one of them the reader sees both fits.
misconceptions: Removes a real unit together with errors it should have corrected
Leaves known errors in the data
Expects a transformation to remove an influence that comes from wrong data and unusual predictors

questions.prompt: You simulate 1,000 replicate years from a Poisson model of leaks per segment and compare them with the observed year. Which comparison can reveal a problem with the model?
options: The total number of leaks
The mean of the fitted rates
The share of segments with no leak
The coefficient of pipe age
questions.explanation: A Poisson model with an intercept reproduces the total by construction; the share of zeros depends on the variation between segments, which the model may get wrong.
misconceptions: Uses a statistic the model matches by construction
Compares the model with itself rather than with the data
Uses a fitted parameter, which replicates do not test

questions.prompt: A logistic model gives a flag a coefficient of 25 with a standard error of 5,000. A cross-table shows that every row with the flag has the outcome. The flag is recorded before the outcome and is legitimate. What do you do?
options: Report an odds ratio of exp(25)
Use a penalised fit, such as Firth's method or a small ridge penalty, and say so
Use HC3 standard errors
Remove the rows with the flag
questions.explanation: The coefficient runs away because of separation; for a legitimate predictor a penalty gives a finite, honest estimate. A flag created by the outcome would instead be removed.
misconceptions: Reports a runaway estimate as a finding
Uses robust errors for a problem of the estimate itself
Throws away the rows that carry the information

questions.prompt: Switching a linear model from classical to HC3 standard errors changes its coefficients as well as their standard errors.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Robust errors change only the estimated uncertainty; the least-squares estimates stay the same.
misconceptions: Thinks a robust variance estimate refits the model

questions.prompt: A model of 60,000 hospital visits in 40 hospitals includes the patient's age and whether the hospital has a new triage system. Which coefficient's standard error is most understated if visits are treated as independent?
options: Patient age, because it varies most
The triage system, because it varies only between the 40 hospitals
Both equally, because all visits in a hospital are correlated
Neither, because 60,000 visits is a large sample
questions.explanation: A hospital-level predictor draws its evidence from 40 hospitals; patient age is compared within every hospital, where the hospital's shared level cancels.
misconceptions: Links the size of the error to the predictor's spread rather than to the level at which it varies
Assumes clustering inflates every standard error by the same factor
Counts rows instead of independent units

questions.prompt: You refit a consumption model with standard errors clustered by district. The programme coefficient was −0.081 with a naive standard error of 0.003. What do you expect?
options: A coefficient different from −0.081 and a standard error near 0.003
The same coefficient and the same standard error, since clustering only matters for small samples
The same coefficient, −0.081, with a much larger standard error
A smaller coefficient, because clustering removes district effects
questions.explanation: Clustered standard errors change only the estimated uncertainty; for a district-level predictor they grow because the evidence is the districts.
misconceptions: Thinks clustering refits the model
Counts rows instead of independent units
Confuses clustered errors with district fixed effects

questions.prompt: A random-intercept model reports a district SD of 0.08 and a residual SD of 0.30 on the log scale. About what share of the variance lies between districts?
options: About 7%
misconceptions: Divides the SDs instead of the variances
Reads the district SD as the share
Multiplies the variances instead of dividing

questions.prompt: In a random-intercept model, a district with 30 bills has a raw mean far above average; its estimated level is about two thirds of that distance from the average. A colleague says the model is "hiding a problem district". What do you answer?
options: The colleague is right; use the raw mean for that district
The shrinkage reflects how little 30 bills say about the district; its estimate borrows strength from the other districts, and more data would move it back if the difference is real
The district should be removed as an outlier
The model should use a larger district SD so that nothing shrinks
questions.explanation: Shrinkage is weighted by how reliable each district's own mean is; it is a better estimate of the district's level, not a cover-up.
misconceptions: Trusts a noisy mean over a pooled estimate
Treats a small district as an outlier
Wants to choose the variance to get a preferred answer

questions.prompt: Clustered standard errors and a random-intercept model can both give honest uncertainty for a district-level predictor, but only the random-intercept model also estimates each district's level.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Clustering corrects the standard errors of the same estimates; the mixed model estimates a level for each district as well.
misconceptions: Believes the two methods answer the same questions

questions.prompt: Before fitting a lasso to forecast summer water demand, you see that the export includes household members' health conditions, which the lasso might find predictive. What do you do?
options: Keep the column and let the lasso decide whether it is useful
Keep it only if cross-validation shows it improves the forecast
Remove it before modelling, because the purpose does not justify processing health data
Keep it but do not report its coefficient
questions.explanation: Data minimisation is decided by the purpose of the processing, not by predictive power; health data is sensitive and not needed for a supply forecast.
misconceptions: Delegates a legal and ethical decision to a penalty
Uses predictive gain to justify processing
Thinks hiding a coefficient makes using the data acceptable

questions.prompt: Which statement about ridge and lasso with standardised predictors is right?
options: Ridge sets some coefficients to zero; the lasso shrinks all of them
The lasso can set coefficients exactly to zero; ridge shrinks them all but keeps every one
Both select the true predictors when the penalty is chosen by cross-validation
Neither needs the predictors to be standardised
questions.explanation: The absolute-value penalty of the lasso produces exact zeros; the squared penalty of ridge does not.
misconceptions: Swaps the two penalties
Thinks a penalty tuned for prediction recovers the true model
Forgets that one penalty treats predictors on different scales unequally

questions.prompt: A lasso selects October consumption in 60% of 100 bootstrap samples. October is correlated at 0.9 with September and November, which are selected 45% and 50% of the time. What should the report say?
options: October consumption is a key driver of demand
September and November should be removed so October is always selected
The autumn months carry similar information and the lasso picks among them unstably; none is reported as a finding
October is significant at the 60% level
questions.explanation: With correlated predictors the lasso's choice within the group depends on the sample; a selection frequency well below 100% is not a finding.
misconceptions: Treats one selection as a stable result
Manipulates the candidate set to force a preferred selection
Reads a selection frequency as a significance level

questions.prompt: A log-consumption model gives programme districts a coefficient of −0.109 with a 95% interval of −0.167 to −0.051. How should the planning report state it?
options: Programme districts: −0.109 (−0.167 to −0.051)
Programme districts used 10.9% less water, which the programme saved
Households in programme districts used about 10% less (5% to 15% less) than comparable households elsewhere
The programme reduces consumption by 0.109 m³
questions.explanation: exp(−0.109) − 1 is about −10%, and the interval converts the same way; the sentence keeps the comparison descriptive.
misconceptions: Leaves the reader a log-scale coefficient
Reads a log coefficient as a percentage directly and adds a causal claim
Reads a log-scale coefficient as cubic metres

questions.prompt: In a capstone defence the assessor removes the household-size-by-band interaction from a log-consumption model. Before re-running, what should you predict for the average effect of an extra person?
options: Every band gets the same percentage effect, so the villa effect in m³ shrinks and the social effect grows towards the average
Nothing changes, since an interaction only affects the standard errors
All effects become zero, because the interaction carried the size effect
The model can no longer be fitted
questions.explanation: Without the interaction one slope on the log scale is shared by every band; the per-band effects in m³ move towards each other, though villas still gain more m³ because they start higher.
misconceptions: Thinks interactions change uncertainty but not estimates
Confuses removing an interaction with removing the main effect
Thinks a simpler model cannot be estimated

questions.prompt: For brief C1, complaints per district-month, a participant fits a Poisson model without an offset. Customers per district range from 40 to 9,000. What does the assessor expect them to fix first?
options: Add log(customers) as an offset so the model describes complaints per customer
Switch to a linear model of complaints
Drop the smallest districts
Use HC3 standard errors
questions.explanation: Without an exposure, large districts have more complaints simply because they have more customers; the offset turns the model into one for the rate.
misconceptions: Abandons the count family instead of adding the exposure
Removes data instead of modelling exposure
Fixes the standard errors of a model whose estimates are wrong

questions.prompt: For brief C2, where the channel of the offer was chosen at random, which statement can the report make?
options: Text messages are associated with uptake, but nothing causal can be said from data
Sending a text message instead of a letter changed the share taking the kit by the estimated difference, with its interval
Text messages work better for every household
The difference is causal only if the model includes every household characteristic
questions.explanation: Random assignment makes the groups comparable, so the difference between channels estimates the effect of the channel for these households.
misconceptions: Applies the caution of observational data to a randomised comparison
Turns an average effect into a claim about every household
Thinks adjustment, not randomisation, is what licenses a causal claim

questions.prompt: A capstone repository whose notebook gives the README's numbers only on the participant's own laptop meets the reproducibility criterion.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Reproducibility means a fresh clone reruns from the raw data with a fixed seed to the same numbers.
misconceptions: Equates running once with being reproducible
